newsitem.title: JAPAN: Gingrich reminds Japan of lingering trade issues.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich reminds Japan of lingering trade issues.

text.p: Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives Newt Gingrich reminded Japan of unresolved trade issues on Monday but assured Japanese leaders that the U.S. Congress was committed to keeping strong bilateral ties.
"Between our two countries, we do have the two issues of aviation and ports," a Japanese Foreign Ministry official quoted Gingrich as telling Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
But Gingrich also assured Hashimoto that U.S. lawmakers were committed to bilateral ties.
"The U.S. Congress will continue with its commitment to Japan-U.S. relations," the official quoted Gingrich as saying.
Gingrich arrived in Tokyo on Sunday for a three-day visit. He is also scheduled to meet Trade Minister Shinji Sato, business leaders and members of parliament.

In reply to Gingrich's statement on trade issues, Hashimoto said Japan does not agree with the U.S. idea of "open skies" -- the dropping of all restrictions on airline operations except for safety requirements.

Hashimoto told Gingrich that Japan would carry out aviation liberalisation step by step, the ministry official said. Japan has asserted that imbalances in the existing aviation treaty signed in 1952 must first be addressed.
"We can expect progress, though, if we continue negotiations in a direction toward getting rid of discrimination," Hashimoto was quoted as saying.
On the quarrel over access to ports, Hashimoto said Japan was trying to resolve this quickly and asked Gingrich to halt U.S. sanctions.

The U.S. Federal Maritime Commission, angry at what it says are costly and discriminatory practices at Japanese ports, said last month it would slap $100,000 surcharges from April 14 on Japanese freighters calling at U.S. ports.
"We are making our efforts. We hope our efforts will not be wasted," Hashimoto was quoted as telling Gingrich.

Japan's politically sensitive trade surplus with the United States edged up in January to $4.29 billion, and some economists fear that the rising surplus and a weakening yen may rekindle Japan's trade friction with the United States.
Hashimoto told Gingrich that his immediate task was to ensure his government could continue leasing private land for key U.S. military bases on the southern island of Okinawa.
"One of the major issues I now face is how to avoid the expiry of the (government's) title to the use of land for the U.S. military," the official quoted Hashimoto as saying.
In his reply, the official quoted Gingrich as saying: "We understand the importance of Okinawa."
Last month, the House adopted a resolution expressing Washington's gratitude to Okinawa for hosting the bases.
Hashimoto faces a May 14 deadline on the expiration of his government's lease on land owned by some 3,000 Okinawans.
The owners of land covering 362,000 sq metres (433,000 sq yards) on 12 bases including the U.S. Air Force's huge Kadena Air Base are refusing to renew the leases.
Hashimoto was poised to push through parliament a controversial new law to ensure his government could continue leasing land for U.S. bases on Okinawa.

Local authorities on Okinawa, where about half of the 40,000 U.S. troops in Japan are stationed, want the bases closed by 2015 but Tokyo strongly such a move. Okinawa hosts more than 75 percent of all U.S. bases in Japan.
